title: Understanding the Mary Fowler Salary: From Hourly Rates to Annual Pay
description: Convert hourly pay to annual salary with the Mary Fowler salary method. Includes National Minimum Wage, tax, super, and award rates for 2026–27.
salarySummary: For a full-time employee working 38 hours per week, the annual gross pay is the hourly rate multiplied by 38 hours per week times 52 weeks.

faqs.q: What is the National Minimum Wage from 1 July 2026?
faqs.a: From 1 July 2026, the National Minimum Wage is $26.44 per hour, $1,004.90 per week for 38 hours, and $33.05 per hour for casual employees including the 25% loading. Award minimum wages also increased by 4.75% from the same date, as published by the Fair Work Ombudsman.

faqs.q: How do I calculate my annual salary from an hourly rate?
faqs.a: Multiply your hourly rate by the number of hours you work each week, then multiply by 52 weeks. For a standard full-time employee working 38 hours per week, the formula is: hourly rate × 38 × 52. This gives your gross annual pay before tax and super.

faqs.q: Does the annual figure include superannuation and tax?
faqs.a: No. The annual gross figure is your base pay. Superannuation is paid on top by your employer at 12% of ordinary earnings (up to the $270,830 maximum contribution base). Tax is deducted from your pay using the 2026–27 resident tax rates and the Medicare levy. The [take-home pay](/topics/take-home) page shows how these deductions affect your net income.

bodyMarkdown:
## The Mary Fowler Salary: A Practical Way to Understand Your Annual Pay

When you hear about the **mary fowler salary**, it’s a handy shorthand for converting an hourly wage into an annual figure. Whether you’re negotiating a job offer, comparing roles, or just curious what your time is worth, the calculation is straightforward: multiply your hourly rate by the hours you work each week, then by 52 weeks. This article walks through the process using the latest Fair Work Ombudsman figures, explains tax and super, and shows how to use the [timesheet](/) to do the maths yourself.

### Why 38 Hours Is the Standard

Most full-time awards in Australia define a standard week as 38 hours. The Fair Work Ombudsman uses this for the National Minimum Wage: from 1 July 2026, the minimum is $26.44 per hour, which equals $1,004.90 per week or $52,254.80 per year (before tax). If you work part-time or casual, the same hourly rate applies but your annual figure will be lower because you work fewer hours. Casual employees also receive a 25% loading – that’s $33.05 per hour – to compensate for not getting paid leave.

To find your own annual gross pay, use the formula:

**Annual gross = hourly rate × hours per week × 52**

For example, if you earn $30 per hour and work 38 hours:

$30 × 38 × 52 = $59,280 per year

If you work 20 hours per week at the same rate:

$30 × 20 × 52 = $31,200 per year

The [hourly conversion](/topics/hourly-conversion) page has more examples and a calculator.

### Award Rates and the Annual Wage Review

The Fair Work Commission’s 2026 Annual Wage Review increased award minimum wages by 4.75% from 1 July 2026. This means many employees under modern awards – such as retail, hospitality, or healthcare – have higher minimum rates than the National Minimum Wage. You can check your specific award in the [pay guides](/blog) or use the Fair Work Ombudsman’s Pay and Conditions Tool. The Modern Awards Pay Database, maintained by the Fair Work Commission, also provides detailed rates for classifications, allowances, and penalty rates.

If you’re covered by an enterprise agreement, your pay may be different. Always check your employment contract or agreement first.

### Fortnightly Pay: A Common Way to Get Paid

Many Australian employers pay fortnightly. To estimate your fortnightly gross, simply double your weekly pay. Using the $30 per hour, 38-hour example:

Weekly: $30 × 38 = $1,140
Fortnightly: $1,140 × 2 = $2,280

Your annual figure stays the same: $59,280. The [reference tables](/data) include weekly, fortnightly, and monthly conversions for common rates.

### Tax and the Medicare Levy

Once you have your annual gross, the Australian Taxation Office (ATO) applies the 2026–27 resident tax rates:

- $0 – $18,200: nil
- $18,201 – $45,000: 15% of excess over $18,200
- $45,001 – $135,000: $4,020 plus 30% of excess over $45,000
- $135,001 – $190,000: $31,020 plus 37% of excess over $135,000
- $190,001+: $51,420 plus 45% of excess over $190,000

Plus the Medicare levy, generally 2% of taxable income. For low-income earners, reductions may apply (using the 2025–26 single reduction thresholds as a guide).

Using the $59,280 example:

Tax on $59,280:
- First $18,200: $0
- Next $26,800 ($18,201 to $45,000): 15% = $4,020
- Remaining $14,280 ($45,001 to $59,280): 30% = $4,284
- Total tax: $8,304

Medicare levy (2%): $1,185.60

Total deductions: $9,489.60

Net annual pay: $59,280 – $9,489.60 = $49,790.40

This is an estimate. Your actual tax may vary if you have HELP debt, the Medicare levy surcharge, or salary packaging. The [take-home pay](/topics/take-home) page provides a more detailed breakdown.

### Superannuation Is Paid on Top

Employers must pay superannuation guarantee at 12% of your ordinary earnings (from 1 July 2026). This is paid on top of your gross salary, not deducted from it. The maximum contribution base is $270,830 per year, so super only applies to earnings up to that amount.

For the $59,280 example:

Super: $59,280 × 12% = $7,113.60 per year

Your total employment cost to the employer is $59,280 + $7,113.60 = $66,393.60. But your take-home pay is still based on the $59,280 gross. Learn more on the [super and packaging](/topics/super-and-packaging) page.

### Casual Loading and What It Means for Annual Pay

Casual employees get a 25% loading on top of the base hourly rate. If you’re casual, do not enter a rate that already includes the loading into the [timesheet](/) – instead, enter your base rate and check the “casual loading” box. The tool will add 25% automatically. For example, a base rate of $26.44 becomes $33.05 per hour casual. Annualised:

$33.05 × 38 × 52 = $65,306.80

But remember, casuals don’t get paid sick leave or annual leave, so the loading compensates for that. The [casual loading](/topics/casual-loading) page explains the trade-offs.

### Using the Timesheet for Your Own Calculations

The [timesheet](/) on this site lets you type your base hourly rate and see the annual, fortnightly, and weekly figures instantly. You can toggle casual loading, and the results show gross pay, estimated tax, Medicare, and super. It’s a quick way to compare job offers or check if you’re being paid correctly.

### A Note on Accuracy

All figures here are based on the Fair Work Ombudsman, Fair Work Commission, and ATO as of mid-2026. The National Minimum Wage and award rates are updated each July. The ABS Average Weekly Earnings for full-time adult ordinary time was $2,083.70 per week in May 2026, which gives an annual equivalent of about $108,352 – well above the minimum, reflecting typical earnings for full-time employees.

If you’re unsure about your award or agreement, check the [minimum wage](/topics/minimum-wage) page or contact the Fair Work Ombudsman directly.

### Summary

The **mary fowler salary** method – hourly rate × hours per week × 52 – gives you a clear annual gross figure. From there, you can estimate tax, Medicare, and super. Whether you’re on the National Minimum Wage, an award rate, or a higher salary, the formula stays the same. Use the tools on this site to run the numbers for your situation.
